extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of analytical geometry, trigonometry, and algebra (advanced/undergraduate and above)
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of propositions, formulae, and procedural rules for analytical geometry in three dimensions, coordinate projections, integration of rational fractions (partial-fraction decomposition via organized division/Horner methods), and practical trigonometric surveying. Provides concrete conditions, algebraic algorithms, and worked examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle between a straight line and a plane
rubrics_metrics.description: The angle required is the complement of that between the straight line and the normal to the plane; if 7', m', n' are projecting coefficients of the line and A, B, C the directing cosines of the normal to the plane, then sin θ is given in terms of these quantities (references to equations (22), (14), (52), (63)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute the angle between the line and plane by taking the complement of the angle between the line and the plane's normal; use the projecting coefficients of the line and the directing cosines of the normal and substitute into the stated formulae. (Surrounding derivation and substitutions are given in the text; see (14, 52, 63).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle between two planes
rubrics_metrics.description: The angle between two planes equals the angle between their normals: expressible by formulas (68) and (69) where the cos and sin of the angle are given in terms of the directing cosines of the normals (A,B,C and A',B',C') and auxiliary functions K, K'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the directing cosines of the normals and substitute into formula (68) for cos Φ and (69) for sin² Φ. The text emphasizes that the required angle is the same as that between the normals, and K-like functions are the same functional form for both sets of cosines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for two planes to be perpendicular
rubrics_metrics.description: Two planes are perpendicular when cos Φ = 0 (and sin Φ = something), leading to an algebraic condition in the directing cosines: (1—f²)A A' + (1—g²)B B' + (1—h²)C C' + (gh—f)(B C' + B' C) + (fh—g)(A C' + A' C) + (fg—h)(A B' + A' B) = 0 (equation (73) and alternative expression (74)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set cos Φ = 0 in the plane–plane angle formulas and simplify to obtain the symmetric algebraic condition; the text also supplies an expanded squared form (74). Use these to verify perpendicularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for a straight line and a plane to be perpendicular
rubrics_metrics.description: A straight line is perpendicular to a plane when the directing cosines of the line coincide with those of the plane's normal (i.e., the line's directional ratios are proportional to A, B, C of the plane's normal).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equate (up to proportionality) the line's directing coefficients (given by combinations like S + A T + g U, etc.) with the plane-normal components A, B, C. The text gives the proportionality conditions explicitly and shows how to derive them from earlier expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for two planes to be parallel
rubrics_metrics.description: Two planes are parallel exactly when the directing cosines of one normal equal those of the other (normals proportional).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare directed cosines; algebraically impose equality/proportionality conditions (reference to (52)). The normals must be scalar multiples of each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition for a straight line and a plane to be parallel (and to lie in the plane)
rubrics_metrics.description: A straight line is parallel to a plane if AS + BT + CU = 0 (equation (77)). If the line lies in the plane, in addition to AS + BT + CU = 0 the coordinates of a point on the line must satisfy the plane's equation (additional condition (78)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: First test AS + BT + CU = 0 for parallelism; to check containment, verify that a point of the line satisfies the plane's equation. Both algebraic conditions are required for the line to be entirely within the plane.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation of a plane through three given points
rubrics_metrics.description: To find the plane through three points (x1,y1,z1),(x2,y2,z2),(x3,y3,z3) set up the linear system for the plane coefficients (N,Q,R,V) satisfying N x_i + Q y_i + R z_i = V for i=1..3; solve for ratios and take 2V as common denominator to obtain explicit formulas (80,81).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve the 3×3 linear system for the plane coefficients; the text supplies explicit determinant-like formulae for the coefficients (80,81) and cautions that the same sign convention must be used in corresponding terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection of a plane area by generators parallel to a given line
rubrics_metrics.description: If φ and ψ are the angles the given line makes with the normals to the source plane Q and target plane P, and R is orthogonal section area, then Q cos φ = R = P cos ψ, leading to P cos ψ = Q cos φ (relation determining the projected area).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model the projection using the cylinder generated by lines parallel to the given line; cut by a plane perpendicular to generators to obtain an orthogonal section of area R, then use R = Q cos φ and R = P cos ψ to relate Q and P.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate projections of a plane area and sign convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Coordinate projections Q1, Q2, Q3 of a plane area Q onto yz, xz, and xy planes satisfy relations involving the directing cosines X1,X2,X3 of the plane's normal (see (84), (85)). The projections must be taken with signs matching the corresponding directing cosines: if a directing cosine is negative, the corresponding projection is negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When computing coordinate projections, ensure Q1,Q2,Q3 carry the same sign as the normal's directing cosines X1,X2,X3; this sign convention affects subsequent formulae (notably (85) and (86)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of a plane surface in terms of its coordinate projections
rubrics_metrics.description: The area Q of a plane surface may be obtained from its coordinate projections by a quadratic relation: Q² = Q1² + Q2² + Q3² − 2Q1Q2 cos α3 − 2Q2Q3 cos α1 − 2Q3Q1 cos α2 (equation (86)), where αi are the angles between coordinate planes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use (85) derived from substitution of directing cosines and simplify to the elegant form (86). Ensure the sign conventions of projections are observed; (86) is presented as a simpler form after applying (70).

rubrics_metrics.name: Area of a plane triangle from three given vertex coordinates (via coordinate projections)
rubrics_metrics.description: For triangle with vertex coordinates given, compute coordinate projection magnitudes q1,q2,q3 via determinant-like expressions (80) and (87); substitute into the area formula (85) to obtain expression (88), taking signs and magnitudes into account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick signs in (80) making qi have same sign as coordinate projections Q1,Q2,Q3 and substitute into (85). The text details how to choose signs so that Q cannot equal −q and explains proportionality to the normal directing cosines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume of a tetrahedron via coordinates and edge inclinations
rubrics_metrics.description: For tetrahedron with origin and points (x1,y1,z1),(x2,y2,z2),(x3,y3,z3), the volume V can be expressed (via preceding notation) and in the special orthogonal case with edges along axes (X,Y,Z) the volume formula reduces to V proportional to XYZ times (1 − f² − g² − h² + 2fgh) where f,g,h are cosines of angles between the three edges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use determinant/triangular area relations (previous propositions) to derive volume; in orthogonal-edge case substitute to obtain the compact expression involving pairwise cosines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organized method for resolving rational fractions (partial-fraction decomposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: To integrate rational functions with factors (a−b)^m etc., perform organized successive divisions: first divide numerator by (x−a)^m as far as the term in (x−a)^{m−1} using direct multiplication of coefficients by 1,2,2^2,...,m^2 (a Horner-like tabular subtraction process), then repeat for other factors in chosen order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write coefficients and multiply rows by 1,2,2^2,... up to required power, subtract sequentially to produce the row of numerators; repeat the process m times. Treat each factor in turn; the procedure is derived from Horner's suggestions and greatly abbreviates computation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for multiple factor divisions and denominator bookkeeping
rubrics_metrics.description: When dividing by a second (or further) factor, reduce prior fractions to a common denominator by multiplying by powers of the new factor, reserve its highest power as a common denominator factor, then proceed with the next factor; nothing beyond necessary low-degree terms in one process will be useful for subsequent ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After obtaining numerators for first divisor, multiply by appropriate powers to align denominators before performing the next set of divisions; reserve common denominator power factors to be reintroduced at the end. The text warns that higher-power terms beyond those useful for later processes can be ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling simple linear factors in partial-fraction resolution
rubrics_metrics.description: If only the first power of a linear factor enters, expunge the factor during the division and restore it after making x equal to its root (i.e., treat simple linear factors by evaluation at the root).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove (expunge) simple linear factors during the tabular division procedure and reintroduce them after substituting x equal to the factor's root to compute the appropriate residue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Horner's method (change of origin) in polynomial expansions
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange polynomial in powers of x−a by substituting x=a via Horner's method before applying the organized division; this simplifies the expansion with respect to factor (x−a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform Horner substitution to rewrite polynomial about the expansion point (root) before the tabular division; this reduces workload and aligns with the organized rule for successive divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trig periodicity and quadrant-shift identities for arcs
rubrics_metrics.description: Relations for sine and cosine when adding or subtracting multiples of semicircumference or full circumference: e.g., sin(pr + A) = ± sin A, sin(gr + A) = ± sin A, cos(pr + A) = ± cos A, etc., for p even/odd and g odd/even where p ∈ {0,±2,±4,...} and g ∈ {±1,±3,±5,...} (equations (3)–(12)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these identities to reduce arcs falling outside a principal quadrant and to generalize sum/difference formulas for all possible arc values; the text uses adding/subtracting multiples of π (semi-circumference) to show universal validity of sum/difference formulae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum and difference formulas for sine and cosine and their universal extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Fundamental identities sin(A±B)=sinA cosB ± cosA sinB and cos(A±B)=cosA cosB ∓ sinA sinB (equations (13)–(16)); the text gives a geometric proof and then extends the validity to all A,B by adding/subtracting multiples of π as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive from perpendicular projections (geometric construction) and then use the periodicity relations to extend to arbitrary signed arcs; the method avoids special-case spherical trigonometry and determines correct signs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveying: height from three elevation angles on collinear stations (case distinction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given three stations D,K,C in a straight line and angles of elevation to object AO at those stations (α,β,γ) with distances between stations known, derive algebraic equations for unknowns (e.g., x and y) that reduce to logarithmic forms (equations (19)–(24)). There are three solution forms depending on relative magnitudes of the angles (cases when α greater than or less than β,γ etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the correct pair of logarithmic equations (19–24) according to the inequalities between the given angles; the text provides step-by-step derivations and an example illustrated numerically. Use logarithms and trigonometric reductions given to compute X and height.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveying: distances from a station to three remote objects given mutual distances and subtended angles
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the three inter-object distances and the angles they subtend at a station S, construct relations for auxiliary variables (h, θ, m) leading to formulas (25)–(29) that determine the station's distances to each object via trigonometric functions and logarithmic computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form equations involving sine and tangent of constructed auxiliary angles, compute h via (25), then θ via (26), and finally PS, RS, QS via (27)–(29). Handle sign cases (e.g., h>1) and choose the correct branch for angle signs as illustrated in the worked example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surveying: distance between two inaccessible objects from observer measurements
rubrics_metrics.description: For computing distance CD between inaccessible objects C and D from angles and a known baseline AB, derive formulas analogous to the three-station problems: introduce auxiliary m,θ and compute h via (30) and tan θ via the given relations; then compute CD from trig relations and logarithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the same strategy as previous surveying problems: set up sine relations for triangle ratios, derive the expression for h and θ, then obtain CD using log-formula for distances. The text gives explicit logarithmic forms and cautions about angle positions and sign choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for finding all three roots of a cubic via a translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a cubic, choose a real root r (by estimation/Horner), diminish the variable by r (i.e., translate), then use the transformed coefficients to compute parameters a and b without solving a quadratic; from these obtain the three roots a±1/β and r. The method yields real/unreal pair characterization via (7₁−7₂)² sign.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Horner to develop the real root to required accuracy; apply the algebraic reduction (shifting by r) to read off combinations that give a and b directly from coefficients (no quadratic needed). Use the provided worked example as template for numeric implementation.
